stops.name: Tarascon, Sainte-Marthe and the Tarasque
stops.campa: Martha, restless in Marseille's shadow, goes up the Rhône to Tarascon, where a beast called the Tarasque, part lion, part dragon, part ox, has been laying waste to the countryside from its den by the river. She goes out to it alone, holy water and a cross in hand, and it lies down before her like a lamb; she binds it with her own girdle and leads it into the town, where the terrified people kill it on the spot and beg her to stay and preach. Mary blesses her sister's going before Martha ever sees the beast, and the two do not meet again in the flesh.

stops.name: The Camargue near Saint-Gilles, the ground before the hermitage
stops.campa: Following the Rhône down toward its mouth, Mary Magdalene crosses a stretch of wild delta country, thicket, thorn, and a clear spring, a country that as yet has no name and no hermit in it. Six hundred years will pass before a Greek exile called Giles finds this same ground, builds his cave beside this same water, and gives the place the name it will keep forever. She does not know she is walking through another saint's future address; the corpus folds its own time here, honestly, the way it must: Giles arrives on her ground long after she has already left it behind.

stops.name: La Sainte-Baume: the grotto, the retreat begins
stops.campa: Above the wooded gorge east of Marseille, in the massif the country will call the Sainte-Baume, the holy cave, Mary Magdalene finds a fissure in the white rock, high above any road, and goes into it to stay. No spring reaches it, no tree grows near it, no herb softens the stone. She leaves the world of preaching and conversion behind entirely, the way she once left Magdala, and gives herself instead to thirty years of a penance so total that the tradition will not even grant her the ordinary mercy of running water.

stops.name: La Sainte-Baume, lifted by angels at the seven hours
stops.campa: Every day at the seven canonical hours, matins, lauds, the day offices, vespers, compline, angels lift her bodily into the air of the cave, and she hears with her own ears the song of the heavenly companies that no living mortal is otherwise permitted to hear from the ground. This is her whole nourishment: no bread, no water, only what the choirs give her at each hour, carried up and set down again like a tide that never wets her feet. A hermit priest, coming near enough once to see it, tells no one for years, not fully trusting his own eyes.

stops.name: La Sainte-Baume, the vision granted to Maximin
stops.campa: Word finally reaches Maximin, now bishop, of the hermit priest's vision, and Maximin comes himself to see: in the cave he watches her lifted the height of two or three cubits from the floor, hands raised among a company of angels, her face lit as though the sun itself were shining through the rock behind her. He understands, watching, that thirty years have very nearly run their course, and that he is not seeing a woman merely fed by heaven so much as a woman being finished by it, made ready at last for whatever door the last hour opens for her.

stops.name: Saint-Maximin (Villalata): the last communion, her death
stops.campa: Told beforehand by the Lord of her approaching end, Mary Magdalene leaves the cave for the last time and comes down to Maximin's oratory at Villalata, the town that will one day take his name. There, angels bear her, one final time, into the church itself, and set her before the altar where Maximin waits with the sacrament. He gives her communion with his own hands; she makes her prayer with her hands joined, and rests in peace. A great brightness fills the whole oratory at her passing, and a sweet odor lingers in the place for seven days afterward, as if thirty years of silence had one last thing left to say.

stops.name: Vézelay: the rival tomb, held unreconciled
stops.campa: A millennium removed from Villalata, a Burgundian hilltop abbey opens a wholly different chapter of the same devotion: the monks of Vézelay declare that they hold Mary Magdalene's true relics, carried north, some say from Aix, some say by a monk fleeing Saracen raids on the Provençal coast, and enshrine them beneath a great new Romanesque nave. Pilgrims by the tens of thousands come to Burgundy believing they kneel before the same bones that Provence also claims to keep whole in its own crypt. Both traditions stand, and neither is debunked here; this corpus does not choose between them.

stops.name: Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume, the 1279 translation of the relics
stops.campa: Two centuries after Vézelay's claim, Charles II of Anjou, count of Provence, comes in person to the crypt at Saint-Maximin and has the tomb opened before witnesses: the skull is found separate from the rest, still bearing, they report, a fragment of desiccated flesh on the brow, where the risen Christ is said to have once told her not to touch him: the noli me tangere kept, quite literally, in the bone. Charles commissions a new Gothic basilica over the site and gives the relic its own reliquary bust. Provence's claim, like Burgundy's, is neither proven nor surrendered; the two tombs simply go on, each keeping its own vigil.
